title: Foundational Imports
content: Imports natural number arithmetic, finite set operations (`Finset`), cardinality, real numbers, the `Irrational` predicate, filters for limits, and general tactics. The formalization bridges discrete combinatorics (finite sets, divisibility) with analysis (limits of density ratios).
mathContext: The formalization uses $\texttt{Finset}$ for finite subsets of $\{1,\ldots,n\}$, $\texttt{Finset.card}$ for cardinality, $\texttt{Filter.Tendsto}$ for $\lim_{n \to \infty} f(n)/n$, and $\texttt{Irrational}$ for the irrationality question.

title: No Divides Two Others (NDTO)
content: Defines the central combinatorial predicate: a finite set $A$ has the NDTO property if no element $a \in A$ divides two distinct other elements $b, c \in A$. This is a weakening of the primitive set condition (no divisibility at all). In the divisibility poset on $\{1,\ldots,n\}$, NDTO sets are strong antichains: elements may have comparable pairs, but no element can be below two distinct others.
mathContext:
$$	ext{NDTO}(A) \iff 
exists\, a, b, c \in A : a \mid b \wedge a \mid c \wedge a 
eq b 
eq c 
eq a$$
Equivalently, each $a \in A$ has at most one proper multiple in $A$. The maximum out-degree in the divisibility graph is at most 1.

title: The Extremal Function f(n)
content: Defines $f(n) = \max\{|A| : A \subseteq \{1,\ldots,n\},\, \text{NDTO}(A)\}$ as the supremum of cardinalities over all valid subsets. This is a Turán-type extremal function for the divisibility poset: how large can a set be while avoiding a specific substructure (an element dividing two others)?
mathContext:
$$f(n) = \max \{|A| : A \subseteq [n],\; \text{NDTO}(A)\}$$
For comparison, the maximum primitive set in $[n]$ has size $\pi(n) + \Theta(n^{2/3}/\log n)$ (Erdős, 1935), while $f(n) \sim 0.67n$ is linear—much larger since NDTO is a weaker constraint.

title: Lower Bound: f(n) ≥ ⌈2n/3⌉
content: The interval $\{m+1, m+2, \ldots, 3m+2\}$ has $2m+2$ elements with $\max/\min < 3$, so each element has at most one multiple in the range. Setting $m = \lfloor(n-2)/3\rfloor$ gives $f(n) \geq \lceil 2n/3 \rceil \approx 0.667n$. This simple construction already nearly matches Lebensold's refined lower bound of $0.6725n$.
mathContext: If $A = \{m+1, \ldots, 3m+2\}$ and $a \mid b$ with $a \neq b$, then $b \geq 2a > 2(m+1)$, so $b \in \{2m+3, \ldots, 3m+2\}$. Each $a \leq m+1$ has at most one such multiple $2a$, so NDTO holds. Density: $(2m+2)/n \approx 2/3$.

title: Lebensold's Lower Bound (1976)
content: Lebensold (1976, *Studies in Applied Mathematics*) proved $f(n) \geq 0.6725n$ for sufficiently large $n$, improving the simple $2/3$ bound. The construction uses a more sophisticated selection of integers, carefully balancing which multiples to include to maximize set size while maintaining NDTO.
mathContext: Lebensold showed $f(n)/n \geq 0.6725$ for large $n$, improving the trivial $2/3 \approx 0.6667$. The gain of $0.0058$ represents the improvement from optimizing beyond simple interval constructions.

title: Lebensold's Upper Bound (1976)
content: Lebensold also proved $f(n) \leq 0.6736n$ for large $n$, establishing that the limiting density lies in the narrow interval $[0.6725, 0.6736]$ of width merely $0.0011$. The upper bound uses a counting argument bounding how many integers can avoid having two multiples in the set.
mathContext: The upper bound $f(n)/n \leq 0.6736$ constrains the density to $\lambda \in [0.6725, 0.6736]$. The interval width $0.0011$ is remarkably tight, yet the exact value remains unknown after nearly 50 years.

title: Existence of Limiting Density
content: Axiomatizes that $\lim_{n \to \infty} f(n)/n$ exists and lies in $[0.6725, 0.6736]$. The existence follows from subadditivity-type arguments for the extremal function, analogous to how densities of other restricted sets are shown to exist via Fekete's lemma.
mathContext:
$$\exists\, \lambda \in [0.6725, 0.6736] : \lim_{n \to \infty} \frac{f(n)}{n} = \lambda$$
The limit exists by Fekete's lemma applied to a suitable superadditive reformulation of $f(n)$.

title: Erdős Problem 1062: Irrationality of the Density
content: States the conjecture: the limiting density $\lambda = \lim f(n)/n$ is irrational. Erdős's question reflects a common theme in combinatorial extremal problems: densities arising from divisibility constraints often turn out to be irrational, suggesting that the optimization landscape is governed by continuous rather than discrete phenomena.

title: Primitive Sets
content: Defines a primitive set: no element divides any other. This is strictly stronger than NDTO. Primitive sets have been studied since Besicovitch (1934) and Erdős (1935), who proved $\sum_{a \in A} 1/(a \log a)$ is uniformly bounded. Lichtman (2022) proved Erdős's conjecture that the primes maximize this sum.
mathContext:
$$\text{IsPrimitive}(A) \iff \forall\, a, b \in A : a \neq b \implies a \nmid b$$
Primitive sets have density 0 (Besicovitch), while NDTO sets have density $\approx 0.67$. The gap reflects the much stronger constraint.

title: Primitive Implies NDTO
content: Proves that every primitive set is NDTO: if no element divides any other, then certainly no element divides two others. This is the only fully proved (non-axiomatized) result in the file, demonstrating the logical relationship between the two conditions via a direct proof by contradiction.
mathContext:
$$\text{IsPrimitive}(A) \implies \text{NDTO}(A)$$
Proof: if $a \mid b$ and $a \mid c$ with $a, b, c$ distinct, then $a \mid b$ with $a \neq b$ contradicts primitivity.

title: NDTO Is Strictly Weaker: The {2, 6, 9} Example
content: Axiomatizes the separation: $\{2, 6, 9\}$ satisfies NDTO (2 divides only 6, not 9; 6 and 9 divide nothing else) but is not primitive (since $2 \mid 6$). This concrete counterexample shows the implication Primitive $\implies$ NDTO is strict, justifying why NDTO allows much larger sets.
mathContext: In $\{2, 6, 9\}$: the divisibility graph has one edge $2 \to 6$. Since $\deg^+(2) = 1 \leq 1$, NDTO holds. But $2 \mid 6$ violates primitivity. Max degree $\leq 1$ (NDTO) vs max degree $= 0$ (primitive) captures the difference.
